entry.title: Flappy Fish: Genetic Algorithm Game
entry.summary: Pygame game where AI fish evolve with a genetic algorithm, with manual play and a deployed demo.
entry.content:
This post is about Flappy Fish, a Pygame-based game where a fish moves through underwater obstacles. The project has a manual play mode and an AI simulation mode where multiple fish learn better behavior over generations. You can try the deployed version at flappy-fish.ai.studio.

What it does

The game uses a Flappy Bird-style loop in an underwater setting: obstacles scroll across the screen, the fish has to pass through gaps, and collisions end the run. Manual mode keeps the gameplay easy to test, while simulation mode lets a population of AI-controlled fish play the same environment automatically.

How the AI learns

The learning part is built around a genetic algorithm. Each fish has a small policy that decides when to flap from state signals like vertical distance from the next gap, horizontal distance to the obstacle, and current velocity. After each generation, stronger fish are selected, crossed over, and mutated so the next generation can survive longer.

Why it was useful

I liked this project because it connects game programming with optimization. The result is visible immediately: changes in the policy, fitness scoring, mutation, or selection pressure affect how the fish behaves on screen. It made the genetic algorithm feel less abstract and more like a system that has to interact with timing, physics, and collisions.

Links: deployed Flappy Fish app and Flappy Fish on GitHub.

entry.title: Cheese Agent: A FastAPI RAG Chatbot with Vector Search
entry.summary: AI-powered cheese agent built with FastAPI, AstraDB vector search, OpenAI, and a lightweight JS frontend.
entry.content:
This post is about my experience building Cheese Agent, a cheese-themed RAG chatbot project with a FastAPI backend, OpenAI embeddings, AstraDB vector search, and a vanilla JS frontend.

What this post is

This is a short technical reflection on building Cheese Agent, especially the parts that made it feel like a real systems project rather than just a UI experiment.

Why I made it

I wanted to build something that combined an interface people would actually enjoy using with a backend architecture that forced me to think about retrieval quality, data organization, and deployment.

How it works

The backend exposes a chat endpoint in FastAPI. When a user sends a question, the backend embeds that query with OpenAI, searches AstraDB, and sends the retrieved context into the generation step.

What I focused on in the implementation

The most useful parts for me were the ingestion script, the vector database, and the split between a simple frontend and a backend that handled retrieval and answer generation.

What seems promising so far

This kind of project is useful because it combines data preparation, embeddings, retrieval, API design, frontend integration, and deployment in one place.

Closing thoughts

For me, Cheese Agent became a compact full-stack AI project where the model, the database, the data pipeline, and the interface all had to line up.
